{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-transpose-product-order}
#### The order of the factors reverses

Transposing a product reverses the order of the factors.
Keeping the original order usually gives an undefined product
or a different matrix.
For example, with $\matr{A} = [1,\; 2]$ ($1 \times 2$)
and $\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ ($2 \times 1$),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A}\matr{B} &= 1 \cd 3 + 2 \cd 4 \\
&= 11,
\end{aligned}
$$

so $\tp{(\matr{A}\matr{B})} = 11$, and

$$
\tp{\matr{B}}\,\tp{\matr{A}}
= [3,\; 4] \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= 11,
\qquad
\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{B}}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} [3,\; 4]
= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

If instead $\matr{A}$ is $2 \times 3$ and $\matr{B}$ is $3 \times 1$,
then $\tp{\matr{B}}\,\tp{\matr{A}}$ is a $(1 \times 3)(3 \times 2)$ product,
but $\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{B}}$ is a $(3 \times 2)(1 \times 3)$ product,
which is undefined.

:::
